blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The Authorization header, holding the bearer token, is logged) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a hash of the token (SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes is enough for high-entropy tokens; no bcrypt needed) in a `token_hash` column, and look a request up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` on the hash of the bearer value — still a single indexed equality, so the lookup stays fast. The clear token exists only in the creation response, shown once. As it stands, anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table — a database backup, a read replica, a support query, an SQL injection elsewhere — gets every user's live credential and can call the API as them (CWE-312 / CWE-256), while passwords in the same database are bcrypt-hashed. Update the design's alternatives and task 1.1 accordingly.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
To diagnose integration problems, the middleware logs each request's
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Never log `Authorization` (nor `Cookie`, `Proxy-Authorization` or any other credential header): redact it with an allow-list of loggable headers, and to identify the token log a non-secret identifier instead — the token row's id or a short prefix of its hash. As designed, every request writes a usable bearer token to the `info` log, so anyone with log access (support, the log pipeline, a log aggregation vendor) can replay it and act as the user (CWE-532); passwords sent through the same middleware by today's integrations would be logged too. Combined with the absence of revocation, a token leaked through the logs cannot be stopped. Change task 1.3 so `logs_requests` asserts the header is redacted.
findings.title: The Authorization header, holding the bearer token, is logged

findings.evidence: - [A user loses a token] → they create another one; revoking the old one comes with the later revocation change.
findings.recommendation: The proposal's own motive is that "a leaked integration exposes the account", yet a leaked token stays valid forever: creating another one does not stop the old one, and tokens have no expiry. Ship at least a minimal delete of a user's own token (server-side ownership check), or an expiry date on each token, with this change; or have a person accept the risk explicitly until the revocation change lands. Confidence is low because the impact depends on when that later change ships.
findings.title: A leaked token cannot be invalidated until a later change
